title: Airstrike

legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y1/Session 6/Airstrike/Case Study_ Airstrike.docx + Guide Notes.docx) is a fictional preemptive-strike scenario, not a real historical event -- unlike Cardiology (a real clinical trial) there is no real underlying dataset to preserve verbatim. What IS real and was extracted and verified: (1) the DIA site-survey coordinate map was embedded in the source docx as an image (a hand-plotted Desmos-style scatter of 9 ICBM and 6 SRBM sites plus Camp Dragonbreath, each site color-coded to one of five warhead classes given in the source text) -- every coordinate and warhead-class pairing in Appendix A was read directly off that embedded image and reproduced verbatim, not invented; (2) the source's stated hardware -- F-16 top speed, the ICBM analog's range and intercept posture, and the SRBM analog's range -- turned out to name or closely match real, checkable military hardware (F-16 Fighting Falcon; a DF-5-class ICBM; the real, since-decommissioned Soviet TR-1 Temp / SS-12 Scaleboard SRBM), so these were fact-checked against real public sources and corrected where the source's number had drifted from reality (the ICBM range was corrected from the source's stated 15,000 km to the real, CSIS-sourced 12,000 km for a DF-5-class missile; the SRBM's 900 km and the F-16's ~2,400 km/h were both confirmed close to real published figures and kept, now cited). What is NOT real and is disclosed as a stated scenario convention in Appendix D: the SRBM intercept rate (5.6%, inherited from the source with no locatable public source for any specific system) and the population-at-risk-by-warhead-class table (Appendix B, inherited from the source's own casualty thresholds, which were themselves plausible-but-uncited narrative figures, not citations to a real study of a real city). The protagonist was renamed from the original source's 'General Kenneth F. McKenzie Jr.' (a real, named former U.S. CENTCOM commander) to the fictional 'General Marcus T. Reyes,' and CENTCOM was replaced with a fictional joint strike cell -- using a real living general's name and real command as the decision-maker in a fictional preemptive-nuclear-strike scenario was judged inappropriate to carry forward into a student-facing case, independent of whether the underlying scenario math changes. Per SPEC.md Section 6's explicit guidance for this exact case ('the math must not require students to optimize human death tolls as an abstract quantity... prefer framings where the stake is protection rather than destruction'), the primary metric was reframed from the source's implicit 'estimate casualties from missiles that get through' framing to 'total expected population protected' -- same underlying arithmetic (site coordinates, distances, times, population-per-warhead-class, SRBM intercept discount), but every deliverable and the balance argument are now stated in terms of what each operation SAVES, not what it fails to prevent. The Twist (three F-16s, not two) was present only in the source's Guide Notes as a one-line stage direction with no mechanical detail ('we can get one more F-16 off the ground') -- this conversion authored the actual mechanism (a 2-minute later launch, a 10-minute window instead of 12) and computed its real effect on the margin from the same coordinate data, rather than inventing a new twist unconnected to the case's numbers.

sources.claim: Nuclear blast radius scales with the cube root of yield; 5-psi overpressure radius anchors
sources.org: Glasstone & Dolan, The Effects of Nuclear Weapons (1977)
sources.title: Effects of Nuclear Explosions -- blast-radius cube-root scaling
sources.note: Well-validated physical scaling law (Sedov-Taylor point-explosion scaling), not an extrapolation for this case's yield range: 50 kt-5.2 Mt sits well within the historically tested/documented nuclear yield range this formula is built from. Anchors cross-checked against two independent public blast-radius calculators (defconlevel.com, nukeblastsimulator.com) summarizing the same Glasstone & Dolan curves used by NUKEMAP.

sources.claim: Representative population density for a 'major urban center'
sources.org: Manhattan Institute, analysis of 2020 U.S. Census data
sources.title: How Large Cities Can Grow Denser and Flourish
sources.note: Average population density across large U.S. central cities, 2020 Census. This is a real, sourced REPRESENTATIVE figure, not a claim about one specific city -- since this case's target city is deliberately unnamed/fictional, real density is genuinely unknowable in advance (the same category as a future price or a medical estimate), not something further research resolves. Real cities vary roughly 3-10x around this average (compare NYC's ~28,000/sq mi to a sprawling metro's low thousands), which is exactly the real-world basis for Appendix B's disclosed P5 sensitivity.

modeling_assumptions.text: Firing standoff distance is a fixed 2 km: an F-16 cannot fire on a target until within 2 km of it, so every leg's flight distance is (raw coordinate distance - 2 km) before converting to time.

SRBM intercept rate is a fixed 5.6%: of any SRBM-class missile that launches, 5.6% is intercepted and 94.4% reaches its target. Inherited from the legacy source with no locatable public source for any specific real system; disclosed as a stated scenario convention, not a sourced figure. This is the case's single most load-bearing assumption -- see case.md Appendix D and sensitivity_model.py.

Population at risk per warhead class (case.md Appendix B: 1,057,614 / 749,145 / 352,364 / 75,915 / 47,823 for 5.2 MT / 3.1 MT / 1 MT / 100 kt / 50 kt) is now DERIVED, not assumed: population = pi*R^2*density, where R comes from Glasstone & Dolan's cube-root blast-radius scaling (S4, a well-validated formula within this case's yield range, not an extrapolation) and density is the real 2020 Census average for large U.S. central cities (S5, a representative figure since this case's 'major urban center' is deliberately fictional). The genuine remaining uncertainty is which real density applies to an unnamed city -- irreducible in the same way a future price or a medical estimate is, not a research gap. A Tier 2 P5 flex check (re-run 2026-08-13 against the derived figures) found the verdict still moves: flexing the 5.2 Mt figure -50% flips the winner to Grey Dawn; flexing the 3.1 Mt figure +50% also flips it. Disclosed in case.md's Balance Argument and FACILITATOR.md's Lessons Learned as a real, sourced sensitivity, not eliminated -- eliminating it would mean silently picking one density and hiding the real range of plausible target cities.

Destroying a missile site before the 12-minute window closes fully protects that site's population-at-risk value (with MA2's discount already applied for SRBM sites). A site not destroyed in time is treated as launching successfully.

deliverables.text: A coordinate table and plotted diagram of all 15 missile sites and Camp Dragonbreath, each site labeled with the quadrant it falls in.
For each F-16 in the chosen operation, the distance in km from Camp Dragonbreath to its first target, and between every subsequent pair of targets on its flight path, using the distance formula.
For each leg from D2, the flight time in minutes (converting km/h to km/min), plus a running cumulative flight-time total per jet, rounded to the nearest tenth of a minute.
Every missile site the operation will not reach in time, and the expected population impact of each one, applying the SRBM intercept-probability discount where it applies.
A bar graph comparing total expected population protected under Operation Grey Dawn versus Operation Desert Sparrow.
A recommendation stating which operation was chosen and why, citing the population-protected totals from D4 and D5.

balance.argument_a: A 2-jet nearest-neighbor ICBM-first route (Grey Dawn) destroys 8 of 9 ICBM sites (88.9%) -- missing only the most distant, ICBM-Golf -- plus 1 of 6 SRBM sites reached with leftover time (9 sites total). Desert Sparrow's own any-target route reaches only 7 of 9 ICBM sites (77.8%), because two legs that should go to ICBM-Hotel and ICBM-Golf get spent on closer SRBM sites instead: on ICBM-neutralization rate specifically, Grey Dawn beats Desert Sparrow by 11.1 percentage points, a 14.3% relative margin -- close to Desert Sparrow's own headline 13.6% population margin, just measured on the undefended threat class instead of raw population. That distinction is real, not rhetorical: ICBM sites carry no intercept discount anywhere in this case's own model (Appendix D's MA2 discount applies only to SRBM sites), while every SRBM site both operations leave standing at least faces a real, sourced 5.6% intercept chance (Appendix C, S2). Grey Dawn leaves just one ICBM site live (352,364 people at risk, undiscounted, Appendix B's derived 1 Mt figure) with zero backstop, trading a smaller population-protected total for eliminating nearly all of the one threat class this region has no real defense against.
balance.argument_b: A 2-jet nearest-neighbor any-target route (Desert Sparrow) reaches 11 of 15 sites total (7 ICBM + 4 SRBM) -- two more sites than Grey Dawn, because it never detours past a closer SRBM site to reach a farther ICBM site. Total expected population protected is a real, computed 13.6% higher than Grey Dawn's total. The real cost is that 2 ICBM sites remain live instead of 1.
balance.margin_basis: Total expected population protected (Appendix B population-at-risk table, SRBM sites discounted by Appendix D's 5.6% intercept rate; ICBM sites undiscounted), summed across every site destroyed by each operation's fastest 2-jet nearest-neighbor route under the 12-minute window. Grey Dawn protects 4,844,636 of 7,830,282 people at risk (61.9%); Desert Sparrow protects 5,918,400 (70.9%) -- a 14.7% relative margin in B's favor. Full computation in sensitivity_model.py and derived{} below.

derived._note: Computed during conversion from Appendix A/B/C/D's own given data via a nearest-neighbor greedy route per jet; case-readiness should re-derive independently, not just trust this block. All population figures are expected values (SRBM sites carry the 94.4%-reaches-target discount from MA2; ICBM sites do not).
derived.p5_flex_note: Re-derived 2026-08-13 after Appendix B's population-at-risk table was rebuilt from real sourced data (S4 blast-radius cube-root scaling, S5 census density) instead of an unsourced convention. python3 skills/case-readiness/scripts/tier2_probes.py --case airstrike --probe 5 --flex 0.5 against the rebuilt figures: base margin 13.6% (was 14.7%); flexing pop_5_2MT -50% still flips the winner to Grey Dawn, flexing pop_3_1MT +50% now also flips it. This is a genuine, sourced instability (the real unknown is target-city density, not the formula) -- disclosed per the P5 disclosure-aware pass criteria, not eliminated.
derived.icbm_neutralization_note: 8 of 9 ICBM sites (88.9%) for Grey Dawn vs 7 of 9 (77.8%) for Desert Sparrow, computed from grey_dawn_2jet_sites_destroyed_list / desert_sparrow_2jet_sites_destroyed_list above -- Argument A's quantitative counter-metric (Tier 2 P2 fix, 2026-08-13, see QA_REPORT.md).
derived.p3_trap_note: The trap: crediting every DESTROYED SRBM site its full undiscounted population-at-risk value (instead of MA4's already-baked-in 94.4%-reaches-target discount, which applies whether a site is destroyed or left standing) still lands on B as the winner but reports a margin of 15.2%, not the real 13.6% -- right recommendation, wrong arithmetic. Computed by re-running sensitivity_model.py's evaluate() with discount_srbm=False applied to destroyed sites only (Tier 2 P3 fix, 2026-08-13, see QA_REPORT.md and FACILITATOR.md's 'The trap').

sensitivity_note: This case's math is framed around protecting population from missile strikes (SPEC.md Section 6's explicit guidance for this exact case), not around optimizing a casualty count as an abstract quantity -- every deliverable states what each operation SAVES. It still carries real weight: a fictional war scenario built on real aircraft and missile hardware, decided by a general who has to choose in minutes. Facilitators should keep the frame on the routing math and the protection framing, and should be ready for a Hero who wants to talk about the ethics of preemptive strikes generally -- that's a legitimate reaction to name and set aside, not to shut down, before returning to the numbers. SEPARATELY, a real Tier 2 P5 assumption-flex check (run 2026-08-13, see QA_REPORT.md) found that Appendix B's population-per-warhead-class table (MA3), not the SRBM intercept rate (MA2), is this case's single most load-bearing assumption: individual class values, flexed +-50%, can flip the winner or push the margin past SPEC.md Section 2's 20% cap. FACILITATOR.md and case.md Appendix D have been corrected to name MA3 as the load-bearing one; a future case-qa Tier 2 run should treat this as already found, not re-discover it.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: Population-at-risk is computed from a validated blast-radius formula (Category I, sourced S4) times a representative urban density (S5) -- but which REAL density applies to this case's deliberately unnamed, fictional 'major urban center' is genuinely unknowable in advance, the same way a future price or a specific future outcome is. No amount of further research produces the one true density of a fictional city.

Same basis as pop_5_2MT: the formula and density source are real and sourced (S4/S5), but which real city's density applies to this fictional, unnamed target is an irreducible forecast-shaped unknown, not a research gap.
